newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Repsol lures investors, paints bright future.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Repsol lures investors, paints bright future.

text.p: Spanish energy group Repsol said on Wednesday it would double its earnings and slash costs in the next five years, tempting investors to take part in the final public share offering of the blue-chip company this month.

There were growing signs of success for Repsol's latest offering as the price of its listed shares on the Madrid stock exchange soared to an intraday high of 6,150 pesetas ($42.37), bolstered by strong demand from foreign investors.
At the first in a series of presentations to Spanish institutional investors, Repsol chairman Alfonso Cortina gave an glowing account of the petro-chemical firm's prospects.

"By the year 2001, Repsol will be a bigger and more profitable company. Total assets will have increased by 30 percent. We think we can achieve earnings on capital employed of around 15 percent and a return on equity of around 20 percent."
"Both operating profit and net profit will have doubled (from the end of 1996 to the end of the year 2001)."
Repsol posted net profit of 119.22 billion pesetas in 1996, only up slightly from 1995.
Sluggish performance by Repsol's chemical division hit the company's earnings in 1996, and operating profit fell to 198.61 billion pesetas from 212.50 billion in 1995.
But the future is much brighter, according to Cortina.
Repsol plans a major investment outlay of 1.6 trillion pesetas up to the year 2001, with the company predicting a rate of return on that outlay of about 17 percent.
"This will be complemented with a cost-cutting programme of around 10 billion pesetas per year, to reach (savings of) of 50 billion pesetas in 2001 versus 1996," Cortina said.
All indications are the share offer will be snapped up by small Spanish investors on the retail tranche, which accounts for about half of the shares on offer, and may be increased, analysts say.

Of the 12.75 million shares available to the public, at the end of the second day of the period allowed for provisional subscriptions, bids were double the shares available, according to local press reports.
Repsol stock already trading has been in demand too.

"More or less everyone is buying, but foreign investors are particularly keen because the stock is liquid enough for them to buy it now on the market rather than wait for the placement," said a dealer who requested anonymity.
The Repsol offer is the latest in a series of hugely popular share offers as the Spanish government continues an ambitious privatisation programme.
A final 20.9 percent stake in Spain's other major multinational, Telefonica, came to the market in February, and bids from small investors outpaced the 114 million shares on offer by nine times.

Repsol executives will make presentations to institutional investors in other European countries and the United States beginning next week. Thirty million more shares will be traded on the market when the offer closes on April 28.
